idiom_name: dedicated creation owner: factory method on the product, standalone factory, or creator registry
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the creation of each aggregate exactly one owner. The factory exposes one named entry point per input shape - a creation path (validated command inputs, fresh identity) and, where persistence exists, a reconstitution path (a raw representation, an existing identity, structural repair rather than business-precondition rejection). Inside, it validates inputs, assembles the object graph, enforces the aggregate's invariants and assigns identity before returning, and the product's own constructor stays private to the factory so no other code can produce an unvalidated instance. Collaborators the creation needs (other aggregates, policies, id generators) are passed in as abstractions, never looked up globally. The factory interface lives in the domain; reconstitution implementations that depend on infrastructure may live in the infrastructure layer. Creation and reconstitution are separate methods with distinct contracts. Prefer returning Result/Either/Option types over throwing exceptions where the language supports it; never return a partially built object.
code_sketch:
order = Order.from_cart(cart, now)        # creation path: new identity, full validation
order = OrderFactory.reconstitute(row)    # reconstitution path: existing identity, repair not reject
# owner internals: validate(input) -> assemble(parts) -> enforce invariants -> assign identity -> return product
pitfalls: Splitting the creation owner (two factories or a factory plus a reachable constructor) lets the two paths drift.
Letting the factory accumulate domain behavior instead of only creation turns the aggregates anemic.
Sharing one entry point between creation and reconstitution; their identity and validation contracts differ.
Injecting infrastructure services directly into the aggregate root constructor to support factory methods, coupling the domain to infrastructure.
Using an ORM's direct hydration (reflection-based population of private fields) as a reconstitution path, bypassing the factory's structural-integrity checks entirely.
Factory doing post-creation work (sending emails, publishing events synchronously, calling external APIs) beyond validating and assembling.
Creating a factory for every value object and trivial entity, adding indirection without encapsulating meaningful creation logic.
A standalone factory that acts as a service but has no domain-side port abstraction for its dependencies, making it untestable without a real database.
Reconstitution factory placed in the domain layer despite depending on persistence-format knowledge (column names, document structure), violating layering.
Round-trip test missing: reconstitute(create(x)) does not reproduce the same state, leaving a gap in validation coverage.

Wrong move: implementing reconstitution as a domain-layer factory class -> it must know column names, document shapes or wire formats to rebuild the aggregate, so persistence knowledge leaks inward and the domain becomes untestable without the storage format -> instead treat rebuilding as data mapping: reconstruct inside the repository or a mapper living outside the domain, and keep only the domain-concepts-only creation factory on the domain side.

Wrong move: exposing one generic create(Object...) that resolves the constructor reflectively by matching argument types -> with two same-arity constructors the wrong one is silently picked and whether invariants ran becomes a coincidence of signatures -> instead give each creation path its own named method that invokes an explicitly validated constructor, and reserve reflective generic creation for trivial products.

Wrong move: a polymorphic creator registry that falls back to a default subtype on an unknown discriminator -> persisted rows or external messages get silently built as the wrong product and downstream rules misfire on plausible-looking objects -> instead make an unregistered type code fail loudly (as fflib's DomainFactory throws when no constructor is mapped) and cover the unknown-code case in the factory's tests.
